newsitem.title: USA: AT&T sees lower earnings in short term, stock tumbles.
newsitem.headline: AT&T sees lower earnings in short term, stock tumbles.

text.p: AT&T Corp. Monday outlined its plans for the local telephone and wireless businesses and said the billions of dollars in investments required would depress earnings in the short run, sending its stock tumbling.

At the opening of a two-day meeting with analysts, AT&T officials said plans to compete in the core long-distance business, and in new areas such as local service, wireless communications and information services, would require investments of more than $8 billion this year alone.

"In the short-term, the investments will put increasing strain on our financial performance," AT&T Chairman Robert Allen said. "These investments put AT&T on a path for powerful growth, but there's no question that they will dilute earnings in the near term."
Industry analysts said they were surprised by the lower earnings forecasts for the nation's largest long-distance carrier.

AT&T said it expected to earn $3.45 a share to $3.75 a share from its core businesses in 1997, compared with $5.6 billion, or $3.47 a share, from continuing operations in 1996, and added that the heavy investments could reduce earnings another 75 cents to $1 a share.
"The earnings targets are incredibly low compared to what we expected," said Frank Governali of CS First Boston.
Analysts had been expecting AT&T to earn $3.25 to $3.45 a share including costs for new ventures and other investments.
"It was somewhat of a shock," said Richard Toole at Merrill Lynch.
AT&T stock tumbled $2.875 to $37 in midday composite trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

AT&T President John Walter said the drop in core business earnings was due mainly to higher capital spending, higher costs for hardware and software from the recently spun off Lucent Technologies, and tough competition to woo consumers.

Walter said plans were still being developed for AT&T to achieve its $2.6 billion in cost cuts over the next two years. That will include the 17,000 job cuts announced last year, of which about 5,700 have been made so far.
But AT&T is also adding employees quickly in new businesses, and ended last year with about 131,400 employees, up about 2,000 from the prior year.
AT&T also warned that if competitive pressures to win consumers' business grow -- or new competitors such as the regional Bell companies jump in -- earnings could even be lower than its forecasts.

Walter said that despite complex technology, regulatory, financial and marketplace demands, the company fully intends to "unleash the power of AT&T and play offence" by continuing to invest in the business.
AT&T was changing to better focus on new areas such as advanced information services and Internet-based electronic commerce, officials said.
Walter estimated the company's capital spending at $8 billion to $9 billion this year and said it would earn $5 a share to $6 a share in five years.
AT&T officials also said first quarter earnings would fall as much as 10 percent from 76 cents a share in the fourth quarter.
The company's 1996 earnings of $3.47 a share were reduced by about 59 cents a share from spending on new businesses such as the local and online markets, officials said.
